lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Fabio Luiz Segura | Lesson 7 -- Presenting the Numbers
lesson.grammar_point: passive voice for presenting data and institutional facts
phases: Who Did It, and Who Cares

listenings.text: A number on its own is not information, it is decoration. Somebody tells me their transaction volume grew forty per cent and I have absolutely nothing, because I do not know from what, over how long, or compared with whom. Forty per cent of a very small number is a rounding error. Forty per cent in a market that grew fifty is a loss of share described as a win. So the rule I give people is simple and it costs one extra sentence. Every figure you say out loud gets a baseline attached to it, in the same breath. From what. Over what period. Against which comparison. If you cannot supply those three, do not use the number at all, because a figure you cannot defend is worse than no figure, and the person opposite you will remember that you could not defend it long after they have forgotten what the number was.

There is a specific thing that happens to people presenting data in a second language, and it has nothing to do with their vocabulary. They read the numbers out and they read them fast, because the numbers are the part they are sure of, and the reading gives them somewhere safe to look. What the room hears is a list. Here is what strong presenters do instead, and you can copy it directly. They say one number, then they stop talking. Then they say what it means. Then they stop again. Two seconds of silence after a figure does more work than any adjective you could put in front of it. And it has a second benefit, which is that in those two seconds you are not speaking, so if the number was hard to say, nobody noticed.

When I look at a bank from an emerging market, I want three numbers and I always get the first two. I get the size of the market and I get their share of it. What I almost never get is the third one, which is the number that tells me how much room is left. Market penetration, in other words. If eighty per cent of the corridor already uses the service, then a very impressive growth figure is about to stop, and everybody in the room can see that except the person presenting. If it is twelve per cent, the same growth figure means something completely different. So when a presenter gives me penetration without being asked, I take them much more seriously, because they have just shown me the number that limits their own story. That is not modesty. It is the strongest thing they can do.
